title: Easter baskets
hookLine: Polish Catholics bring food to be blessed on Holy Saturday

lines: A QUIET CHURCH ON HOLY SATURDAY.
cards: Holy Saturday morning, in a Polish parish. The church is strangely quiet; there's no Mass during the day.
But the aisle fills anyway, with families carrying wicker baskets lined with white cloth and tucked with sprigs of green.
Inside: a few painted eggs, a piece of sausage, a heel of bread, a little salt, a spoonful of horseradish, and often a small lamb made of sugar or butter. The baskets go in rows on long tables.
A priest comes down the line with holy water and a prayer, spattering the cloth, the eggs and a few delighted children.

teach.h: THE CHURCH WAITS AT THE TOMB.
teach.b: First, the day. The Roman Missal describes Holy Saturday as a day when the Church waits at the Lord's tomb, and there's no Mass until the Easter Vigil after dark.
Into that quiet, families bring their food: a small act of hope, setting out the Easter meal before Easter has come. Second, the name.
In Polish it's święconka, the blessed food, used for the basket and for the custom.
Contents vary by family, and people give them meanings as they pack: eggs for new life, bread for Christ the bread of life, salt for what preserves and gives taste, the lamb for the Lamb of God.

Those meanings are tradition, passed on at kitchen tables, not rules. Third, the blessing. The Church has blessings for food at Easter, and a priest or deacon asks God to bless the food and the people who will share it.
It's grace before meals, written large: the whole Easter table lifted up before anyone eats. Last, the meal. The basket goes home and waits.
On Easter morning, families share its food at breakfast, often starting by passing a blessed egg around the table.

In John's Gospel, in a breakfast you met in your first year, the risen Jesus stands on a beach at dawn beside a fire with fish on it, and says to his tired friends, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come, and dine."
Risen from the tomb, in this story, he makes breakfast.

how: On Holy Saturday, Polish Catholic families, in Poland and in Polish parishes elsewhere, bring baskets of Easter food to church to be blessed by a priest or deacon, then share the food at breakfast on Easter morning.

games.q: your basket has just been sprinkled with holy water on Holy Saturday. when does the custom say you eat it?
o: right away, on the church steps.
after the Easter octave is over.
games.why: it goes home and waits through the night. on Easter morning the family shares it, often starting by passing a blessed egg.

practice: Bring to mind a table you'll sit at soon: who will be there, and what will be on it. See one dish covered with a white cloth, waiting while you wait too, and notice what it's like to prepare a feast before its reason has arrived.
If you pray, ask God to bless that food and the people who'll eat it; if you don't, give thanks for them, one by one.

wordCard.voice: Easter baskets. Baskets of Easter food, eggs, bread, salt and more, brought to church on Holy Saturday to be blessed and shared at Easter breakfast. In Polish, święconka. Today's word.

orig.note: Polish, the blessed food: both the basket and the Holy Saturday custom.

carryVoice: Your line: święconka. The Easter food, blessed while the Church still waits. Rest well.
